text: A Subflow is reusable Flow Designer logic you call from other flows — it is not triggered directly by a record event or a schedule the way a top-level Flow is. In this lesson we'll nail down exactly when to reach for one.

Under the hood, a Subflow lives in the same table as a regular Flow, sys underscore hub underscore flow, just with a type flag marking it as a subflow. It uses the same triggers, actions, If-Else blocks, and For Each loops you already know from Chapter 2 and Chapter 3. The one structural difference is that a subflow has no Trigger of its own. It never starts on its own — it only runs when a Flow, or another Subflow, calls it.

Here's the test that actually decides it. Ask yourself: does this logic need to react directly to something happening in the platform — a record created, a field changing, a schedule firing? If so, build a top-level Flow, because only a Flow has a Trigger. Or does this same sequence of steps need to run from more than one place — called after different triggers, inside different flows? If so, build a Subflow, write the logic once, and let every flow that needs it call it by name.

Picture three flows already built in an instance: onboarding, offboarding, and an equipment-request flow. All three, at some point, need to notify a manager that a decision is needed and log whatever that manager decides. Build that inline in all three flows, and you've pasted the same five or six steps in three places. The first time someone needs to fix the notification wording or the logging step, they have to find and update it three times — and it's extremely easy to update two and forget the third. Extract that logic into a single Subflow called Notify and Log Manager Decision, and all three flows call it instead. Fix it once, in the subflow, and every calling flow picks up that fix immediately, with zero changes to any of them. That said, subflows aren't automatically the better choice — if logic is triggered by one specific event and nothing else needs that same sequence, a plain top-level Flow is still correct.

Build a Flow when something reacts directly to an event. Reach for a Subflow once you can point to real reuse. Next, we open up what a subflow actually passes back and forth with the flow that calls it — its Inputs and its Outputs.
